Our Response: We thank the reviewer for carefully identifying these grammatical and phrasing issues. The manuscript was thoroughly proofread.

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
This manuscript by Huang and colleagues describes the function of a gene product, DspII, that is involved in production of cis-2-decenoic acid. It's thorough and the experiments are logical and logically presented. There are a few issues:

Our Response: We thank the reviewer for the positive feedback and insightful suggestions.

1. The figures are quite challenging to read with very small text and in cases where there are multiple lines (eg, 3B,5B, etc.) these are difficult to distinguish. Figure 3A - it is impossible to discern what the authors are showing.

Our Response: Thanks for the comment. These figures were revised to improve readability using curves with distinguishable colors.

2. The discussion of Pel in PAO1 is misplaced. (Lines 154-181). The decrease in transcription is marginal. Pel is not known to contribute to biofilm formation in PAO1, so it's not clear at all what is being shown by the authors here.

Our Response: Thanks for the comment. We agree with the reviewer that Pel is not the major EPS for biofilm development in PAO1. Since both Psl and Pel are known to contribute to the biofilm development in non-mucoid P. aeruginosa, we also included Pel for examination. Our result confirmed that CDA induces biofilm dispersion by repressing the expression of Psl genes. We now explicitly state that CDA-induced biofilm dispersion occurs primarily through repression of Psl, consistent with the knowledge that Psl is the primary EPS used to develop biofilm and maintain its structure in PAO1 (Colvin et al., 2012).(Lines 182-183)

3. Lines 191-193. Why this PDE from D. oryzae?

Our Response: Given that native PDEs might coordinate with other cellular activities and thus exhibit regulatory function independently of changing the intracellular c-di-GMP content, we chose to confirm the role of c-di-GMP by expressing an exogenous PDE W909_14950 from D. oryzae, which has been well-characterized and demonstrated to function efficiently in P. aeruginosa to lower c-di-GMP levels in our previous study (Zhou et al, 2022), to eliminate unexpected effects might be caused by native PDEs. The reason for using this exogenous PDE was added: “we expressed an exogenous PDE W909_14950 (14950), which is from Dickeya oryzae EC1 and has been well-characterized and demonstrated to function efficiently in P. aeruginosa to lower c-di-GMP levels without nonspecific effects28” (Lines 207-209).

4. Lines 212-225. FleQ deletion is known to abrogate Psl production in PAO1. The fact that it does so in the DspI/II strains does not make it follow that FleQ mediates CDA's induction of Psl.

Our Response: We thank the reviewer for highlighting this overstatement. To test the role of FleQ, we exogenously added CDA to WT and ΔfleQ strains and measured Psl expression. CDA reduced Psl expression in the WT but not in the ΔfleQ mutant (New Figure 4L), confirming that FleQ is required for CDA-mediated repression of Psl. (Lines 235-236)

5. Lines 341-354. There is no evidence presented that the components have to be in complex to achieve the production of CDA. It's an inference the authors make, but it does not support the assertion (line 348-349) that the "direct interaction is essential for the chronic-to-acute switch".

Our Response: Thanks for the comments. We predicted the structural model of DspII-DspI complex and confirmed the interaction between DspII and DspI by mutating critical residues (R57/R96/E231/R232) in DspI for their interaction (New Figures 8D, 8E, 8F). We further demonstrated that the ΔdspI mutant was unable to synthesize CDA as well as regulate biofilm dispersion, swarming motility, and T3SS gene expression with the complementation of the DspI variant DspI# (DspIR57A/R96A/E231A/R232A) (New Figure 8G, 8H, 8I, 8J). These newly obtained results supported that direct interaction is essential for the chronic-to-acute virulence switch. (Lines 393-404)

6. Issues of word choice or language -
- line 19-20. There is no such thing as a "process of virulence"
- line 39 - pathogenesis does not undergo development
- line 51 - what is compounded?
- lines 88-89 - 25.81 - 40.16% is overly precise.

Our Response: We have carefully addressed all the language issues pointed out by the reviewer throughout the manuscript.

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
The manuscript titled “Dual-Functional DSF-family Quorum Sensing Signal Synthases DspII and DspI Coordinate Chronic-to-Acute Virulence Switch in Pseudomonas aeruginosa” is interesting. This manuscript is about the molecular mechanisms of the chronic-to-acute virulence switch in Pseudomonas aeruginosa, dual function of the DspII-DspI complex, Enzymatic: biosynthesis of the quorum sensing signal cis-2-decenoic acid (CDA) as well as non-enzymatic: direct regulation of gene expression (T3SS) via promoter binding, Regulation of c-di-GMP and its effect on biofilm and motility, Interaction between the Gac/Rsm regulatory system and DspII/DspI. And finally, the Importance of quorum sensing in bacterial pathogenicity and adaptation.

The experiments design is robust based in the use of gene knockouts, gene expression assays, protein-DNA binding assays, cytotoxicity tests, and Galleria infection models. Moreover, it will be able the therapeutic potential by identifies novel targets to prevent the transition to acute infection.

Our Response: We thank the reviewer for the positive feedback and insightful suggestions.

The figures are well organized, with clear labels and explanatory legends. But, there are some defects or inconsistencies:
- Figure 3d (c-di-GMP modulation by CDA): Although a reduction in c-di-GMP is shown, it is not quantified with additional controls (e.g., independent PDEs) to distinguish whether CDA acts directly or via global regulation.

Our Response: Thanks for the comment. There are at least 42 DGCs and PDEs which probably participate in the metabolism of c-di-GMP in P. aeruginosa. We examined the expression of all known DGCs and PDEs in the ΔdspI mutant and only those with expression changes > 20% were focused and further verified, which led us to determine the rbdA as a critical one upregulated by CDA to decrease c-di-GMP content. However, we were unable to precisely quantify the involvement of other potential DGC or PDE in modulating the c-di-GMP pool in the presence of CDA and it is of high possibility that CDA modulates c-di-GMP metabolism via global regulation. We have discussed this: “Notably, our screening result revealed that, apart from RbdA, several other DGCs and PDEs including those known to modulate c-di-GMP content exhibited expression changes (Supplementary Table 1). This finding highlights the intricate regulatory network through which CDA influences intracellular c-di-GMP dynamics via global regulation with RbdA as the main player. Future investigations could explore the involvement of additional DGCs and PDEs targeted by CDA, as their collective actions may contribute to the chronic-to-acute virulence switch.” (Lines 461-465)

- Extended Figure 4a (protein purification): SDS-PAGE gels of DspII and DspI purification are shown, but no molecular weight marker is labeled. This makes it difficult to confirm band purity or expected size.

Our Response: SDS-PAGE gels of DspII, DspI, and their variants including molecular weight markers were shown in New Figure S7.

- Figure 6b (protein-DNA interaction, EMSA): The observed shift for DspII appears subtle and may raise doubts about binding strength, but the article does not discuss this limitation in detail.

Our Response: We agree with the reviewer that all EMSA results showed a weaker binding affinity between PrsmZ and DspII than PrsmZ and DspI. During revision, we found that the catalytic sites of DspII and DspI are important for DNA binding (as shown in the new EMSA result in response to the first comment from Reviewer #1, New Figure 7G). Since DspII only has one catalytic site Glu143, while DspI has two catalytic sites Glu126 and Glu146, fewer catalytic sites in DspII explains its weaker DNA-binding affinity than DspI. (Lines 357-365)

- Final schematic model (Fig. 7):
• It summarizes the proposed mechanism well but does not include:
• The biphasic effect of CDA (as described in the text).
• The unresolved indirect repression of RsmY, which the article

Our Response: The model has been revised to include the biphasic effect of CDA (enhances DspII-DspI interaction and inhibits the binding of DspII and DspI at PrsmZ) and the newly discovered repression mechanism of RsmY (direct binding of DspII and DspI with GacA) (New Figure 9).

- Lack of structural validation: No visual information is presented on the DspII-DspI structure or interaction predictions, which would strengthen the functional complex hypothesis.

Our Response: We employed HDOCK and PLIP servers to predict the interaction of DspII and DspI and introduced mutations of the critical residues predicted for DspII-DspI interaction. The newly obtained results (New Figures 8D to 8J) not only identified the critical residues to support the interaction between DspII and DspI but also confirmed the importance of the interaction in synthesizing CDA and modulating the virulence switch. (Lines 393-404)

- No images of the infection model (Galleria mellonella) are included in the figures, which could have provided direct visual evidence of the virulence phenotype.

Our Response: Representative images of the G. mellonella larvae following 14-h inoculation of P. aeruginosa strains were shown in New Figure S5.

Moreover, I have some general comments to take in consideration of the authors:
1. Unresolved indirect regulation of RsmY: repression is observed, but the underlying mechanism remains unclear. Please, the authors must elucidate the indirect repression mechanism of RsmY by DspII/DspI.

Our Response: As also suggested by Reviewer #1, we tried to further explore the repression mechanism of rsmY by DspII and DspI. We excluded the possibility of binding at PrsmY by the DspII-DspI complex (New Figure S9A) and preventing GacA’s binding to PrsmY by DspII or DspI (New Figure S9B). While surprisingly, we found that DspII/DspI can directly interact with the GacA protein (New Figure 7H), which reduces the transcriptional activity of GacA and thus inhibits the transcription of rsmY. Together, we are now able to show the mechanism of how DspII and DspI antagonize the GacA-dependent induction of rsmZ and rsmY. (Lines 366-378)

2. High specificity of the CDA control system to P. aeruginosa, which limits its generalization to other species. To explore additional downstream targets of CDA: such as other PDEs, DGCs, or effectors involved in c-di-GMP modulation.

Our Response: We screened all the known DGCs and PDEs and then verified the contribution of those with expression changes > 20% to regulate biofilm dispersion (Table S1). Only RbdA was confirmed as the critical one that mediates CDA’s regulation on c-di-GMP metabolism. However, the contribution of all the DGCs and PDEs was hardly to be precisely determined. Considering the expression of multiple DGCs and PDEs are influenced by CDA, it is of high possibility that CDA modulates c-di-GMP metabolism via global regulation with RbdA as the main player. We have discussed this in Lines 461-465. With regards to the effector, we have examined all 12 known effectors in P. aeruginosa and found that FleQ is the target effector that mediates CDA’s regulation on biofilm dispersion and swarming motility (Figure S3).

3. Low sequence similarity between DspII and DspI, raising questions about the evolutionary basis of their functional interaction

Our Response: Thanks for the comment. Low sequence similarity between DspII and DspI suggests that they originated from an ancient gene duplication event. To provide evolutionary basis for their functional interaction, we performed distribution and evolutionary analysis (New Figure S10), which showed that the dspII-dspI gene clusters are confined to three specific clades, meaning that the gene cluster was formed on at least three independent occasions in evolutionary history. We added this result and discussed that the occurrence of the dspII-dspI gene cluster implies a strong selective advantage potentially reflecting a pre-existing functional synergy between two proteins that was stabilized and enhanced through coordinated, localized regulation (Lines 443-452).

4. Determine the prediction structure by bioinformatics tools of the DspII-DspI complex to understand their interaction and CDA-dependent regulation.

Our Response: We employed HDOCK and PLIP servers to predict the structure of the DspII-DspI heterocomplex and generated mutations at the critical residues that are predicted for DspII-DspI interaction. The new results (New Figures 8D to 8J) not only identified the critical residues to support the interaction between DspII and DspI but also confirmed the importance of the interaction in synthesizing CDA and modulating the virulence switch. (Lines 393-404)

5. The authors could Investigate clinical applications: such as inhibitors of DspII/DspI or their interaction to prevent acute virulence switching.

Our Response: We thank the reviewer for this forward-looking suggestion. We fully agree that our findings may open up new therapeutic avenues. As now detailed in a new paragraph in the Discussion section (Lines 507-520), we discuss the potential of targeting the DspII-DspI complex. We propose two main strategies: 1) inhibiting CDA synthesis or degrading CDA to prevent CDA-mediated dispersion, and 2) more promisingly, disrupting the protein-protein interaction itself to simultaneously block both CDA production and T3SS activation, thereby "locking" the bacterium in a less virulent state. We also outline our future direction to screen for such inhibitory compounds. We believe this addition significantly strengthens the translational impact of our work.
